maintopic: MR. EZRA BUTLER EDDY BESSEY.
speechtext: I would ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), if he has considered this Bill. It is a proposition to change the name of a person born in the province of Quebec, and does the Minister of Justice think that such a Bill comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament? I am of opinion that such a Bill would fall within the jurisdiction of the province in which the register of the birth of the gentleman is kept, and the registers are carefully kept in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: MR. EZRA BUTLER EDDY BESSEY.
speechtext:
In looking over this Bill I was under the impression that it came more properly within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature as a matter of property and civil rights. However, I do not wish to raise any objection to the Bill going through, as I am aware that the young man will be a gainer by about three quarters of a million -dollars if he gets his name changed within two years after he becomes of age. i knew his father and grandfather very well, and I have no desire to see any objection raised to the Bill. I had not thought of the point raised by the right hon. gentleman the leader of the opposition; there may be something in it. It is quite possible the young man was born in Hull, of that I have no knowledge. But as his parents resided in Hull at one time, I have no doubt the right hon. gentleman may be

quite correct. I fail to see, however, that that is a material point.

maintopic: MR. EZRA BUTLER EDDY BESSEY.
speechtext: I would be sorry to do anything that would injure the prospects of this young gentleman. I also knew his family and grandfather very well. I have no desire whatever to interpose between him and the rights which he is to obtain under the will of his grandfather. But the very suggestion my hon. friend now makes is one which is in the interest of the young gentleman himself, because, if we pass an Act here that we have no power to pass, we might seriously interfere with his prospects.

BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 115), to provide for the Extension of the Boundaries of the province of Manitoba. He said:	Mr. Speaker, when the
resolutions upon which this Bill is founded were in Committee, the hon. member for Mr. PELLETIER.
Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), asked that we should lay upon the table of the House a map showing the boundaries as proposed; I have done that and have also handed to my hon. friend a copy. This map has been prepared by the geographer, and I believe it shows accurately the boundaries as proposed by the resolutions, and by the Bill of which I now move the second reading.
I might also give to the House some information as to the population within the added territory as furnished to me by the officials who have charge of the census. The population is as follows:

It is thus apparent that there has been very little settlement and1 apparently very little development in the territory which is thus to be added to the province of Manitoba. However, we cannot tell what development may come in the future. We know that the Hudson Bay railway is to be constructed, and we also know that the government of the province of Ontario have it in mind that the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway will, in the course of time, be extended through a portion of this territory so as to reach a port on Hudson bay.
The boundaries now proposed are the same as those which were affirmed by this House on the 13th day of July, 1908. I might state that between 1905 and 1908, the province of Saskatchewan laid claim to some portion of the territory which is now proposed to be included within the boundaries of the province of Manitoba. That was alluded to by the then Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in moving the resolution I have just mentioned, on July 13, 1908. He used this language as expressing the conclusion which the government had reached in that connection:
After giving due consideration to this claim on the part of the province of Saskatchewan, it seemed to us that, as between the claim of the province of Saskatchewan and of the province of Manitoba, to have the territory which lies north of Manitoba and east of Saskatchewan allotted either one way or the other, the weight of argument was certainly in favour of Manitoba and we could not grant the prayer of Saskatchewan. We therefore had to ignore it.
The present administration has seen no reason to depart from the conclusion which was thus arrived at.

Objection was taken during the debate on the resolutions to certain financial provisions which were then proposed, and which are embodied in this Bill. Criticism was directed against the date at which these financial provisions shall take effect. I need not remind the members of the House that the claim of Manitoba for an extension of its boundaries is of long standing. It was said, and I think accurately said, by the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), when he was moving the resolutions in 1908, that that claim dated as far back as 1884. It was renewed with a good deal of insistance in 1901, and as far as I am able to understand, it was proposed or suggested at that time that the claim of Manitoba in that regard should be postponed until what were then the territories lying west of Manitoba should be formed into provinces. Those territories were constituted into the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan during the session of 1905. The right hon. gentleman who then lead the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) dealt with the claim of Manitoba in that regard1 when he moved, the first reading of the Autonomy Bills. He spoke of the claim of Manitoba to an extension of its boundaries as one which was entitled to fair and just consideration, but he attempted to justify the delay in dealing with that particular matter by saying that it could not be properly dealt with until Ontario and Quebec, and also the new province of Saskatchewan, then being constituted, had been consulted. Subsequently to that date Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec were consulted, and the result was the proposal of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), embodied in the resolutions of July 13, 1908. The suggestion is made that although Manitoba put forward a claim which was entitled to consideration in 1905, but which claim was not acceded to at that time for the reason already allud'ed to, a delay of some six years having intervened, Manitoba should have no consideration whatever, for the time which has intervened between 1905 and the present time. I am not disposed to accept that conclusion.
I have already said that Manitoba urged, and urged with great insistence, that inasmuch as her claim should have had consideration in 1905 it would be proper, and only just and fair, that whatever financial provisions were to be embodied in the Bill providing for an extension of her boundaries, should date not from today, but from the period in 1905 when the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were first constituted. We have not seen fit to date these financial provisions so far back as that, but we do think inasmuch as the boundaries which are 136i
now proposed were unanimously affirmed by this House in 1908, that it is no more than just to the province of Manitoba that those financial provisions should date and take effect from the 1st day of July 1908, and we ask this House to support us in that conclusion. What are we giving to Manitoba? We are increasing the lands indemnity from the sum of $100,000 to $562,500, the same as to Saskatchewan, and estimated on the same basis as in the case of that province. But we have asked Manitoba to accept, and Manitoba has agreed to accept, a deduction of $149,230 from that sum, leaving the net amount to be received by Manitoba in respect of her public lands of the sum of $413,370. Now my hon. friend the member for Kd-monton (Mr. Oliver) has put the case very strongly in that regard. I do not know whether I quite apprehend the point of my hon. friend, but apparently he thinks that we are not giving Manitoba quite sufficient compensation in respect of her public lands, because I observe that in the course of his remarks on that question in the debate on the resolution, he declared that Manitoba has restored to us swamp lands which are worth at a fair calculation $21,000,000 in capital or $1,000,000 a year in annual revenue. While I do not accept the computation of my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) I think there is at least enough in his argument to justify us in saying that the proposal to which we are now asking the assent of the House does no more than ordinary simple justice to the province of Manitoba. After all, Mr. Speaker why should there be any discrimination between the province of Manitoba and the province of Saskatchewan in that regard? It is perfectly true that Manitoba was constituted into a province in 1871, and that Saskatchewan was constituted into a province in 1905, but everyone of us realizes also that the financial position of this Dominion is different to-day from what it was in 1871, and that consideration can properly, and in the public interest ought to be, extended to the province of Manitoba to-day which it was not possible to extend to that province when it was first constituted in 1871. And I venture to think that a proposal which takes away and removes any discrimination between the enlarged province of Manitoba and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, is after all one which is eminently in the public interest, one which is entirely justified by every sentiment of fair-play and one that should appeal to every member of this House. Further than that, Mr. Speaker, I need not allude to the fact that Manitoba is handing back to us these lands of which a detailed statement was given upon the introduction of this resolution, except to bring the testimony

of my right hon. friend who leads the opposition to the value of the asset which the Dominion of Canada is receiving in the return by Manitoba of these lands. Speaking in the debate upon the Autonomy Bill in 1905, at page 1439 of ' Hansard' of that year the right hon. gentleman said this:
The swamp lands are perhaps the most valuable lands in the province of Manitoba. They require some preliminary work for drainage but when drained there are no better lands in the whole province. When the late government gave to the province of Manitoba th-j swamp lands they made her a valuable gift, and it has proved to her a most important asset.
Well, Manitoba, in qonsideration of the financial arrangements exactly similar to those made for Alberta and Saskatchewan, is handing back to us the swamp lands, the very great value of which have been urged by the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, and by the member for Edmonton. We have charged Manitoba with every dollar which she has received out of these swamp lands, less the cost of administration, we have also charged Manitoba with 150,000 acres of land granted to the University of Manitoba. These stand in a somewhat different position from the swamp lands, because, when these lands were granted to the university, the province of Manitoba had no control over them as I understand. They were dealt with for the University of Manitoba, and so far as the sale of them is concerned the proceeds accrue to the university and not to the province as a whole. We have thought it only fair and reasonable, therefore, that value should be deducted as on the date, or about the date, when they were first granted. That value has been estimated at $2 per acre. So that the total amount in respect to which Manitoba accounts to the Dominion for the lands granted to the University of Manitoba is the sum of $300,000, upon which interest at the rate of 5 per cent has been deducted. But it may be asked, why should Manitoba or any other province receive compensation from the Dominion of Canada in respect of lands that are held by the Dominion, and are not administered by the province? Well, the principle upon which we are proceeding to-day was adopted by the late administration in 1905, when it fixed the financial terms for Alberta and Saskatchewan. Therefore, I do not suppose that any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House will be disposed to quarrel with that principle to-day. In fact it has already been recognized so far as Manitoba is concerned, because to-day, before the Bill passes, Manitoba is receiving, or would receive, $100,000 annually, in respect of these public

speechtext:
lands, or as an indemnity for the lack of them. But I would like to point out the very great revenues which other provinces in Canada are receiving from their public domain to-day. The amounts that I am giving to the House have been taken from the very valuable yearbook or handbook, published by Mr. J. Castell Hopkins, and I am quoting from that handbook for the year 1911. According to Jcnat authority New Brunswick received in the year 1910, for what is termed territorial revenues, the sum of $494,491.64. In the same year the province of Nova Scotia received from its mines, $629,010, and from its Crown lands, $33,600, making a total received by the province of $662,610, from public domain which is not possessed by the province of Manitoba, or by the province of Alberta or Saskatchewan. The province of Quebec, in the same ye_ar, received in respect of its lands and forests $1,150,747, and from its mines, fisheries and game the sum of $182,132, a total of $1,332,897, from its public domain. In the same year the [DOT]province of British 'Columbia received from timber leases and licenses the sum of $2,325,000, and from land sales and revenue '$887,600, a total of $3,212,600. In the same year according to the authority, the province of Ontario received from its lands, forests and mines, $2,951,428. I have no doubt that in every. one of these cases some expenses and costs of administration must be deducted, and I am merely pointing out that the province of Manitoba, and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, in being deprived of their public domain, which is being administered by Canada and for the benefit of Canada, so far as any revenue is concerned, are certainly entitled to some consideration in respect of subsidy for the withdrawal of those lands.
It is upon this principle, the principle acted upon in 1905, that we proceed today when we ask parliament to sanction this increased allowance to the province of Manitoba. Now, it may be asked, Why should we give compensation at all? Why should we not permit Manitoba to retain its swamp lands? Why not hand over to the province all the Crown lands within the enlarged boundaries and thus place the province in the same position as the other provinces of Canada except the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan? Well, it has been thought best- and I apprehend there is>
good reason for the conclusion-that the matter should be dealt with at one and the same time so far as Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned. But the delay that will be involved in carrying out such an arrangement is surely no good reason why there should be delay in doing that jus-

tice to Manitoba which she has long claimed. It is for that reason that we think it is no more than right, in the first place, to put Manitoba upon the same financial basis and to accord to her the same financial terms as those which have been already accorded to the sister provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Because, I repeat once more, these three provinces stand in a different category from the other six provinces of the Dominion. The other six provinces have their natural resources, their public domain, mines, minerals and other assets of that kind; these three provinces have not those assets. Having in regard these considerations our policy and our proposal is, in the first place, to put Manitoba upon the same just and fair basis as that which has already been granted to Alberta and Saskatchewan, and then to take up, at the earliest opportunity, the question of the terms upon which the natural resources of all three prairie provinces shall be handed over to the administration of these provinces. And I would like to repeat what I have already said in speaking upon the resolutions in that regard, that when we do come to consider that pronosal I think it will be just and necessary to give some consideration to the maritime provinces whose boundaries cannot be enlarged by reason of their natural situation, to call them into our councils and give to them a just voice as to the terms upon which these lands shall be ha-ided over, and especially with regard to what compensation, if any, should be given to the three maritime provinces by reason of the transfer of these lands to the governments of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Now, what else do we propose so iar as Manitoba is concerned? We propose to increase the annual allowance on account of debt from $178,947.65 to $381,584.19. Alberta and Saskatchewan each receive an annual allowance on account of debt of $405,375. We have made certain just deductions in the case of Manitoba which have already been fully explained to the House upon the resolutions. Why should there be any discrimination between Manitoba on the one hand and Saskatchewan and Alberta on the other in this regard? Shall the accident of the date of the establishment of these provinces make any difference in that respect? My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) declared with a great deal of earnestness that inasmuch as Manitoba was constituted in 1871 and Alberta and Saskatchewan were not constituted until 1905, Manitoba had no just and reasonable claim in this regard; because, he said, Manitoba is an old province in this confederation, established forty years ago. I would submit two or three considerations to my hon. friend from St. John and to the members of this House. In the first place, these three provinces differ from all other provinces in Canada in this respect-that they are not provinces which originally constituted this confederation and they were not sovereign provinces at the time of confederation, but brought in afterwards. Each one of these three provinces has been carved out of territory that was added to this confederation shortly after 1867. Therefore, so far as that is concerned, and except for the accident of dates, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan are precisely in the same category.
But my hon. friend from St. John declares that the circumstance to which I have alluded, that accident if I may so call it, constitutes a valid reason which should prevent us to-day from giving to the province of Manitoba the same consideration in respect of debt allowance that was given in 1905 to Alberta and Saskatchewan. I aim bound to say that I do not so regard it. Every one of us knows, who has been familiar with these transactions, that Manitoba in 1905 pressed her claim to have her boundaries extended as far west as Regina. We know that the government of that day did not see fit to entertain that claim. But suppose that claim had been entertained, suppose the boundaries of Manitoba had been extended as far west as Regina or further, would my hon. friend from St. John say that no increased allowance in respec^of debt should have been granted' to Manitoba in that regard ? Surely he would not say that. Manitoba is having her boundaries extended to-day. The debt allowance is based upon the consideration of population, in the ease of Manitoba as in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Manitoba in 1905 wanted her boundaries extended. Would my hon. friend from St. John be prepared to say that if the territory so far west as Regina had been constituted into a province it would have been quite right to make for that province a special, generous debt allowance, such as was granted under the Act of 1905, but that if the same territory had been added to Manitoba, no such consideration should have been given to Manitoba by reason of the population, within that added territory? It does not seem to me that the argument of my hon. friend is consistent with the attitude taken by his leader in 1905 and by the government of which he was at that time, or very shortly after, a member. So we have come to the conclusion that the debt allowance of Manitoba should be placed exactly upon the same basis as that which was adopted in 1905 with regard to Alberta and Saskatchewan when they were constituted into provinces.
Now, so far as the terms of the Bill are concerned, hon. gentlemen on. both sides

of the House, are, no doubt, familiar with them. Sections 1 and 2 are of a formal character. Section 3 sets out the bourn-daries, sections 4 and 5 deal with the financial terms and set forth in considerable detail the items of increased allowance which we propose to make to the province of Manitoba by the Bill. Section 6 provides that the Crown iLands and all the public domains shall continue to be vested in the Crown and administered by the government of Canada for the purpose of Canada, subject to the provisions of any Act of the parliament of Canada.
Section 7 deals with the rights and properties of the Hudson's Bay Company. Section 8 provides that the province shall continue to be represented in the Senate of Canada by four members, provided that such representation may, -after th>- completion of the decennial census of June, 1911, be increased to 6 by the parliament of Canada. Section 9, the last section, provides that the Act shall not come into force until proclaimed by the Governor in Council, and that such proclamation shall not be made until the legislature of Manitoba shall have assented to the provisions of this Bill.
I, therefore, Mr. Speaker, submit the , Bill with every confidence to the members of this House in the hope and in the expectation that it will receive their approval; and in the confidence that they will regard it as no more than a simnle act of justice to the province of Manitoba in respect of claims of long standing, which some of us at least think should have been considered, and should have been regarded, and should have been granted long before this date. So far as the arrearages are concerned, on which the argument of my hon. friends opposite principally spent itself in the debate of a few days ago, I say that inasmuch as the province of Manitoba had every reason to ask that its boundaries be extended in 1905, and inasmuch as these boundaries, exactly as they are proposed to-day, were defined by resolution of this House on the 13th of July, 1908, parliament is doing no more than a simple act of justice When it declares that these terms shall take effect and date, not from to-day, but from the 1st day of July, 1908.

I do not think that any one in this House will be disposed to admit that the right hon. gentleman who leads the government has made out good ground for, in effect, making the provisions in respect of these financial terms to be granted to Manitoba, retroactive, and giving the province a lump sum of about $2,000,000 to represent what would have been the increased allowance from the 1st of July, 1908, supposing the same terms had been arrived at at that time. Now the only ground stated by my Mr. BORDEN.
right hon. friend is, that this parliament- I think it was this House, not the parliament-passed resolutions in favour of extending the boundaries of Manitoba in 1908. Now, Mr. Speaker, that was not the conclusion of the bargain. That was an effort on the part of this parliament to extend the boundaries upon certain terms, which were not agreed to by the province of Manitoba; that is all. Nothing was carried to a conclusion, nothing became binding upon the Dominion and the provinces, but everything remained uncompleted until the present time. Now upon what theory does my right hon. friend date this provision back to the 1st July, 1908? He says to-day we are now giving these improved financial terms to Manitoba as a part of the plan for the extension of the boundaries, and because Manitoba is assuming jurisdiction over this added territory. That is one of the grounds which my right hon. friend puts forward for giving to Manitoba these improved financial terms. Well has Manitoba during these four years been charged with anything in connection with the administration of the government in the added territory? -Not at all. Has she been called upon to bear any burdens? Not at all. Has she built a courthouse, has she erected a public building, has she built a road, has she established a school district, has she incurred one single dollar of liability in the added territory? Not one. Yet my right hon. friend is asking this parliament to vote $2,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada to the province of Manitoba absolutely without a particle of consideration. It does seem to me that it is utterly impossible to justify that provision of the Bill.
Now then my right hon. friend puts it forward as a ground for the passing of this Bill that this parliament passed certain resolutions in 1908, and therefore, because Manitoba did not accept the terms,. and this government is now asking parliament to grant new and more favourable terms, which are now to be accepted, the whole arrangement should date back, and Manitoba should get compensation for the four years delay. Well, my right hon. friend has placed upon the order paper resolutions foT the extension ot the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec. The resolutions, providing for these extensions were also passed in 1908, and what compensation does my right hon. friend propose to give to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, because those resolutions were not carried into effect in 1908, and Ontario and Quebec have not had the use of the lands which would have been given them in 1908? Does my right hon. friend propose to apply the same principle to these provinces? He could, with just as much reason. But he could not do it at all, because there is no reason upon which he could found such a proposition in re-

spect of either Ontario or Quebec; and what reason can be advanced for giving financial terms to Manitoba to date back to 1908, which cannot equally be urged in favour of Ontario and Quebec? Can we suppose that the people of Manitoba would ask for anything out of the treasury of this country to which they are not fairly entitled?
Now then my right hon. friend has called attention to the next provision of the statute in relation to the allowance which he says is by way of compensation for the province not getting these lands. He also dates that back to 1908. I think this is the first time that it has been put forward seriously that a money allowance is by way of compensation for lands. That is not the way in which it was put when the $100,000 was first allowed to Manitoba; it was put as being in lieu of lands; in other words, because the province was not given the lands from which it would have a revenue; therefore it was desirable to give it a money grant to enable it the better to carry on the administration of the affairs of the territory. But it was never recognized that the province of Manitoba or any other province of Canada is entitled to the public lands. Those lands, the land in the territories, the land in Prince Rui-pert's land, the land of all the territories, was bought by the original four provinces of Canada, by Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, I do not think Prince Edward Island was then a member of the confederation.

speechtext:
I think a reading of the whole of the remarks of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, made at that time, bears out what I say. _
My right hon. friend did not put it that the province was entitled^ to the public lands, but he put it that inasmuch as the provinces were not going to have these lands as a source of revenue, it was proper to give them money which woul'd take the place of the revenue that they would get from the lands. That is the way in which it was put in the statute thirty years ago
when $100,000 per year was granted; it was for want of public lands and not as compensation for lands. I say again, and I say it with confidence, that it has never been recognized by parliament that the provinces were entitled to these public lands. They are the l&nds which belong to the Dominion of Canada, which belong to New Brunswick, Nova bcotia and Prince Edward Island, just as much as they do to Manitoba, Ontario, or Quebec, and the matter must, it seems to me, be dealt with from that standpoint. As I have said, they were bought by the money of the people of Canada and the people of Canada have the right to be considered, and the various provinces have the right to be considered, in the disposition which shall be made of these public lands. I grant that in the case of Ontario and Quebec there is an exceedingly strong argument in favour of the placing of the public lands in the control of the provincial governments just as the lands in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec as now constituted are under the control of the provinces, but at the same time, in connection with the placing of the land under the control of the provinces, the rights of the other provinces are entitled to be considered. So, I say that in the case of Manitoba, we have the right to deal with the matter from the standpoint that the province of Manitoba has no claim to these lands in the territory which is to be added, but it is a question as to what amount of revenue from the Dominion treasury shall be granted to the province by reason of the fact that it is not to get these lands as a source; of revenue. \vnat I especially object to is that the government to-day is picking out one of the provinces of Canada and proposing to accord to it special treatment without paying attention to the rights of the other sections of Canada. I am not opposed to treating Manitoba not only fairly but generously, I am not opposed to giving Manitoba, out of the Dominion treasury all the money which is needed to enable it reasonably to carry on the administration of affairs within the province. I think it is the duty of the Dominion, as far as possible, to give such aid to all the provinces of Canada as will enable them fairly to discharge the duties devolving upon the governments of the different provinces. It is one thing for the great family of provinces to sit down together and consider what is right and fair to all and it is another thing for the government to pick out a certain province and bestow upon that special favour. The only argument which I have heard from the right hon. leader of the government and the only argument that I heard from the hon. Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if Manitoba wants more money to enable her to carry on the affairs of government, and to properly develop her territory, we ought to do the same as was done in 1885; we ought to readjust the debt account as between the different provinces. We should endeavour to treat all fairly. It seems to me further, that we should try to make an end1 of the matter as between the different provinces; we ought to have it embodied in the British North America Act, and make it as nearly final as it is possible to make it. Picking out first one province and then another and dealing especially with it, and so tinkering from time to time with the constitution is exceedingly unsatisfactory, and is likely to cause great discontent as between the people of the different provinces. I want to know why my right hon. friend and his colleagues do not consider the whole question now. Take the case of British Columbia. British Columbia is not nearly as favourably situated as Manitoba will be when this Bill passes. British Columbia is growing with equal if not greater rapidity than is Manitoba, and there is no reason in the world why British Columbia should not receive- equal treatment. But my right hon. friend may say: we will deal with British Columbia by itself; the government of British Columbia has demanded that a commission in the nature of arbitrators shall be appointed to deal with the claims which that province is putting forward; the government of British Columbia has demanded that there shall be appointed three commissioners, one to be chosen by the federal government, one by the government of British Columbia, and the third to be appointed by the commissioners so chosen, and, as appears in the press despatches, the federal government has consented to leave the case of British Columbia to that arbitration. I submit that is exceedingly unsatisfactory. What is to be done in respect to the claims of the other provinces of the Dominion? Are there claims to be dealt with by a commission; are they to have similar special treatment? We have had no intimation so far as to what treatment is to be accorded to the three old provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince EdL ward Island. The people of these provinces have borne the burden connected with the development of conferedation, the building of the Canadian Pacific railway and the construction of other public works for the benefit of the whole country. They have borne their share of the burden cheerfully with the Test of the people of Canada, but I do not observe any indication on the part of this government that their special claims
are to be considered. Is there to be a commission of inquiry as to what claims they have on the public treasury? We have no announcement as to that, but what the government is doing to-day is picking out the one province of Manitoba, giving to it special treatment, and proposing to pick out British Columbia, and through the medium of a commission, accord to that province special treatment as well. In considering this question of debt account, it might be well to deal for a few moments with the basis upon which the debt account of the provinces was provided for by the Act of Confederation. In the case of the four original provinces, the debt account was something tangible; it represented something. In the case of Optario and Quebec, the two original provinces, they had actually expended at the time of confederation, sixty-seven million dollars, for which they were in debt, and this was afterwards discovered to amount to seventy-three million dollars. They had built the great canal system of which Capada is so proud, and which was even then a great system, although it has since been vastly unimproved; they had built other public works and they had incurred this indebtedness actually. The province of Nova Scotia at the time of confederation had built a line of railway from the city of Halifax to the New Brunswick boundary and it had constructed the Windsor branch and other portions of what is now the present Intercolonial railway system. Nova Scotia went into the Dominion with a debt account of eight million dollars, which was actually expended upon public works, and all of which were to be passed over to become the property of the Dominion. After confederation in 1869, it was discovered that between the time of the Quebec conference and the coming into force of the Act of Union, the province of Nova Scotia had expended a very considerable sum which had not been taken into account when the debt was fixed at eight millions, and subsequently the debt account of that province was increased from eight millions to over nine millions. At that amount it remained until 1885, when there was a general pro rata increase of debt allowance among the different provinces of Canada by the statue to which I have referred. ! But, that debt amount did not represent paper as this allowance to Manitoba does. That amount was allowed to the province of Nova iScotia because Nova Scotia had actually gone into debt, and constructed public works to that extent, which were transferred to the federal government. parliament can authorize the government of Ontario to build its railway in the territory of another province. I doubt that, Mr. Speaker. I do not think there can be any ground for that contention, because while I think parliament might authorize a company to build a railway there, and undoubtedly it could, yet the government of Ontario cannot construct a railway without public money; and I think it goes without saying, that this parliament could not empower the province of Ontario to expend the public moneys of that province in the construction of a railway which the legislature of Ontario itself could not authorize.

It would be a most anomalous proposition that this"parliament snould authorize the government to pay provincial money for the construction of a public work which the legislature of the province itself could not authorize. Now, I did not intend to take up so much time; I regret that I have spoken at such length upon this subject. But it is one of a great deal of importance, one, I think, of vast importance. I think we ought not to deal with the matter by piecemeal. We are brought to-day by this Bill, face to face with very important changes in the constitution ' of several provinces. We are called upon to consent to the enlargement of the boundaries of the provinces. Important questions are raised. It does seem to me that the only satisfactory way in which these questions can be dealt with is to treat all the provinces of Canada as being interested in them. All the provinces to-day are interested in the public lands. Ail the provinces, of course, are interested in the amount of money that is given by way of subsidies. The only satisfactory way in which to deal with that is to call together the Premiers of the different provinces, just as was done in 1906, and ask them in consultation with this government to take up all these questions, all questions which are outstanding between these provinces, and reach a settlement upon some broad national basis which will relieve all grounds of dissatification and cause all the people to feel that complete justice has been done to each province and to the people of Canada as a whole.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is the second day that this very important measure has been brought to your attention and the attc-nt'on of the House. On each occas-

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: Suppose the time should come in the next two or three years when these lands will be surrendered to the provinces, would the hon. gentleman consider that this allowance in lieu of land should be discontinued?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
It has been my habit in public life to cross bridges when I come to them. I apprehend that one will soon
be reached, and then I propose to give it as earnest consideration as I give to other questions. The chief point against which the attack of the opposition is directed is the other item of increased advance, namely, allowance in lieu of debt. Now, I may be pardoned if I trace the history of this allowance, and the reason for it. It has been done at different times in this parliament, but not very fully in this debate. When the four provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec formed confederation in 1867, Upper Canada, comprising the latter two, was burdened with an indebtedness of some $67,000,000. That indebtedness was incurred for similar purposes as the other provinces have incurred indebtedness, which the other provinces incurred since that time, and have to bear themselves. Now I have stated that very briefly, and I do not intend to particularize, just what that money was expended for. But I say it will be clear to every member of this House that in the main that indebtedness which at that time burdened the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada and burdened the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, was in the main incurred for those public works, for those public purposes that otherwise would have had to be borne, and have been borne since in the case of the other provinces, by the local exchequer.
Recognizing that, the fathers of confederation came to an understanding. I should have sftated that the debt thafs was at that time carried by New Brunswick was some $7,000,000, and that the province of Nova Scotia carried a debt of some $8,000,000. It was figured out by the framers of the Quebec resolutions, and then by the framers of the British North America Act, that the debt of Ontario at $67,000,000 was greater per capita than the debt of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at $8,000,000 and $7,000,000 respectively. It was proposed that United Canada should take over these obligations and relieve the provinces and in order to reduce the per capita debt taken over by United Canada to the same basis in the different provinces $5,000,000 of the debt out of $67,000,000 was left standing on the shoulders of the two provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, and in the ultimate a debt of $7,000,000 for New Brunswick, $8,000,000 for Nova Scotia, and $62,000,000 for Upper and Lower Canada was assumed by. the confederation under this agreement in 1867. It was fixed at these figures in order that the debt assumed from the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec, would represent in a word $25 per head of the population. When, therefore, these four provinces came in, Canada assumed a per capita debt of $25 per head. Later on other obliga-

tions from the provinces were assumed by the confederation and the per capita debt was enlarged to $32.43 per head. At the time that was done a rearrangement among the provinces of the debt allowances was made in order to adjust that of each to the changed circumstances. We have thus proceeded on the assumption from confederation, or from a date prior to confederation, that the per capita debt of the provinces, which was found to be $32.43, should form the basis of a system of allowing to new provinces who might join later and thus share in the national burden, a compensation from the federal treasury when such provinces at the time of uniting had themselves no debt for the union to assume. So when new provinces were brought into confederation, by virtue of the Act of Canada alone, by virtue of the Act of this House, and it was found that these provinces, or territories then erected into provinces, had a less debt than $32.43 per head, or no debt, allowance had to be made in respect therefor. Manitoba came into confederation without any debt at all. Her debt, at the time she entered confederation, was nothing, and consequently it was assumed that the debt allowance to be made by Canada should be on the full basis of $32.43 per head of the population. The same principle applied when Alberta and Saskatchewan entered the confederation.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: Is not my hon. friend mistaken? It was not on the actual population of Manitoba, but on an assumed population of 125,000, was it not?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
I think that in the first place it was on a population of 17,000, but afterwards, in 1885, it was increased to the figures stated by my hon. friend. But, the point will not help my friend: it rather assists the argument that I hope to advance. In the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan, however, the population was figured, when they came into confederation iii 1905, to be 250,000 in each province. That '250,000, multiplied by $32.43, amounted in the aggregate to $8,107,500, and that was the capital allowance made in lieu of debt made to Alberta and Saskatchewan. Manitoba had come in in the earlier years at a time when her population was very sparse indeed, and the allowance in lieu of debt had necessarily to be figured on a smaller amount of population. Later on, as Manitoba advanced in population, that allowance was increased, as the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who has just interrupted me, says. But, what I want to point out is that a distinction between the allowance in lieu of debt has to be made by virtue of the fact that whem new provinces come into confederation they Mr. MEIGHEN.
thereby assume a share of the liability of confederation proportionate to their population, whereas, if they had remained out of confederation they would have had no share in that liability. Parliament set to work to do away with that obvious unfairness and the way it adjusted it was this, and it seems to me that if not exactly right the arrangement was conceived in a. spirit of fairness and at the time approximated thereto. Parliament has made a grant to each such province of five per cent yearly on its debt capitalization; that is to say, each province has entered confederation on a capital debt allowance represented by its population multiplied by 32-43, and five per cent per annum thereon has been granted as a subsidy in lieu of debt to each of these provinces. As we apprehend the ground work of this allowance in lieu of debt, we will come to more clearly understand this legislation in the case of Manitoba and whether or not a re-adjustment should take place in this case or any othe^-without a conference of the provinces. While the debt allowance was conceived in a spirit of fairness, and with an effect approximating thereto at the time, it will be seen that with the unequal advance of population in each of the provinces an unfair condition is certain to result. Had it turned out to be the case that each province had remained at the population it had when this debt allowance was made then the conditions should always have been fair and just between them. Had it even transpired, as may possibly have beep expected, that each province would advance proportionately in population, that is to say, that the advance would be at the same ratio in each, then likewise, the allowance in lieu of debt might have been said to have been on a permanent basis and have remained permanently fair between them. But, such has not been the case. Manitoba wag taken in with a very small population. It advanced rapidly. Manitoba came in with about 15,000 of a population, and she has to-day nearly 500,000. She bears the proportion of the national debt of this country that her present population bears to the population of Canada; that is to say she carries the burden now that her population bears to the whole population of Canada and not the burden that the population when she came into confederation bore to the whole population then. So it will be seen that with the unequal advance in the population of the provinces of this country a distinctly disjointed state of affairs arises in so far as this allowance in lieu of debt is concerned. I need only remark ffiat if no readjustment is to be made in lieu of debt, as the right hon. leader of the opposition argued in 1908, and as the hon. member for St. Johu argues now, and as the now loyal opposition in 1908 distinct-

ly said to the province of Manitoba, in these words: ' We will not even discuss this question with you in regard to your allowance in lieu of debt-if that position is to be taken, it would mean that the province which came, in and opened its arms to confederation in its younger life, came in when its population was sparse, would be at a disadvantage and its tax-payers would be suffering a very decided wrong when its population had advanced out of proportion to that of the older provinces. No argument that is rooted in right, or fair-play can be advanced that this allowance in lieu of debt is part of the compact of confederation and would be subject to no readjustment at all.
In my judgment-I argue this from a conviction that it is right-the allowance in lieu of debt-that constituent of the subsidies by the Dominion to the provinces-is just as much and just as necessarily subject to readjustment as is the allowance in lieu of land'. That ie to say, that as the provinces increase in unequal degree and in unequal proportion in their population, a readjustment must necessarily be made on the basis of that increase, and that, I submit, can be fairly made as has been done in the past, by this parliament without conferences. The right hon. the leader of the opposition, and I think the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), will recognize the truth of what I say when I say that the principle I now argue for, of a readjustment from time to time of the allowance in lieu of debt has been recognized by the House before, not once, but five times, without any reference to a conference with the provinces. The allowance to Manitoba itself, in lieu of debt has been increased in 1871, in 1873, and up to 1885. The allowance in lieu of debt has'been adjusted by this House from time to time as population advanced in unequal measure. And never, that I have heard, has objection been raised to it, because it was not preceded by a conference with the provinces. Why, that very Act of 1885, from which the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), quoted, whereby the allowance to Manitoba was increased by a very substantial amount at that time; was not preceded1, so far as I have been able to find out, by any conference with the provinces. If the present Bill is in any way a violation of an infringement of the compact of confederation, the Act of 1885, was certainly the same. The Act of 1885, purported to put the subsidy to be granted to Manitoba on a footing that would, up to that time, do justice to the province of Manitoba. The government of the day thought that justice to Manitoba was not being done by virtue of the tremendous increase that Manitoba's population had undergone, and the larger share 137
she bore of the obligations of Canada, and the parliament in 1885, finding that to be the case, thought it would do justice to Manitoba. All that is asked at the present time is that this parliament of 1912, should do the same justice to that province.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: In 1885, was it not simply a proportionate increase among all the provinces, Manitoba included?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: The Act I read, and I am sure it is correct, is an Act respecting Manitoba alone, and the Act is headed: An Act to Increase the Subsidy to Manitoba and1 adjust- all claims up to date.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: Was not that in 1884 and not 1885?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) told me it was in 1885.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: There are two Acts, one iri 1884 and one in 1885.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: That only adds strength to my argument.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I was quoting from the chapter in the revised statutes which, as I understand it, is the statute under which the provinces were increased proportionately.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I asked the hon. gentleman and he told me that it was a transcript of the Act of 1885.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I thought it was. It says it is subject to all claims up to the first of January, 1885, so that it may have been in 1884.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
If it was adjusted in 1884 and also in 1885 it will hardly be open to the hon. gentleman to argue that no adjustment must take place without conference. The Act of 1885 is entitled an Act for the final settlement of the claim made by the province of Manitoba on the Dominion, and it proceeds to deal with the matter section after section. The first section grants the swamp lands to the province; the second section grants this one hundred and fifty thousand acres of university lands, the third section increases the indemnity for want of public 'lands, which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) uow argues should never be done unless you call a conference of the provinces. The next section was a readjustment of the per capita allowance of the province, out of a sense of justice by this parliament, and so on all down the line. Therefore, Manitoba's subsidies were revised in 1885, and revised in deference to the fact that Manitoba's population had increased so as to bring about an injustice to herself in the



subsidies she was then receiving from the Dominion treasury, and which were altogether less than she was entitled to receive on account of her population. At that time Manitoba was bearing her share of the obligations of Canada; she was paying her share of the public debt of Canada in proportion to her then population and not in proportion to the population that she had in 1870, when she entered the family of provinces. If there is any fault in my reasoning which I am unable to apprehend myself, I would be glad to have it made known to me now. I say that the allowance in 'lieu of debt, the allowance in lieu of public lands, and the other allowances are all on the same footing, and that they have from time to time been adjusted by this parliament without conference, and solely out of consideration for the existing circumstances. I say that the very circumstances that demanded their readjustment in days gone by, demands with louder voice their readjustment now. And, there is an added reason for their readjustment now, in that, in the case of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, this principle has been recognized and since then the taxpayer of Manitoba has borne an undue share of the burden relative to the taxpayer of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Every reason that existed in 1885 exists now, and to-day we have the plainer, the clearer, the more specific reason in the fact that this parliament recognized that right of Alberta and Saskatchewan to subsidies in 1905 to which in all justice we are entitled as being exactly on the same footing in confederation.
I think I have covered each and every item in the proposed rearrangement. The arrearages are dated back to 1908 by way of compromise, as I understand. In so far as our right to equality is concerned, they *could with all justice, date back to 1905. But it is quite true that we have not been carrying during these years the burden of the extra administration of the northern lands, and consequently I think it was only fair to make a deduction from these arrearages and that a fair compromise was struck in selecting the first of July, 1908, about which date parliament recognized the right of this province to a readjustment of its terms and of its territory.
As to the allowance in lieu of debt, it is justified by all the reasons that have justified this parliament in days gone by in making similar readjustments and it is further justified by the action of this parliament seven years ago.
The justice of the allowance in lieu of lands is admitted by the right hon. gentleman himself who in 1908 clearly placed his government and his party in the posi-Mr. MEIGHEN
tion of being ready to make an increased allowance to Manitoba in lieu of public lands. As to the other features of the arrangement there is no objection. So unless hon. gentlemen opposite can find some graver objection to this Bill than objections to its financial terms I fear they are not going to gain much capital in the country on that ground.
What is the cry of the Liberal opposition in the legislature of Manitoba? The provincial opposition represents in miniature the opposition in this House, they stand on the floor of the local House to-day and say that Manitoba is not getting nearly enough and that they are going to appeal to the people of Manitoba on the ground that the rights of that province have not been adequately acceded to by the parliament of Canada. And, perhaps not on exactly the same grounds but on a similar one, an hon. member of the local opposition, Mr. Mol-loy; has stated on the floor of the local legislature in language that carries us back very closely to 1885, that until justice is done to Manitoba and the west the cry of secession and the demand for secession will increase with emphasis until it cannot be denied and yet his Menus in this parliament are endeavouring to stir up jealousies among the provinces on the ground that Manitoba is getting too much.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: Was Mr. Molloy in the local House dealing with the question of better terms for Manitoba when speaking in that way?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I said that he made this statement on the ground that Manitoba and the west were not being properly treated in the confederation.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: It had nothing to do with this subject at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
I do not know how much reference Mr. Molloy had to this subgect, but I know that the member for Lakeside stood beside Mr. Molloy and doubtless received his applause when he said that he would not be satisfied with the terms granted to Manitoba by this Act but would fight on for better terms. That is to say the opposition in that province is conducting what they believe is a vigourous campaign at this very hour against this Bill on the ground that it does not do justice to our little province and the opposition in this House, professing the same principles, ready to link arm in arm with the local opposition in the same campaign, resist the Bill because it is unjust to all other provinces in confederation.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
Mv hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) dealing with the subject of the Bill before the House, made the point as he sat down, that the financial terms of the Bill must be fair and reasonable, because the opposition in Manitoba were complaining that those terms were not sufficiently liberal to the province, while the opposition in this parliament, were complaining that the terms were too liberal. My hon. friend is under the impression that a great many other people are under, that it is not possible for a bargain to be bad for both parties to it, just on the same principle as some people are under the impression that no bargain can be good for both parties to it; that under normal conditions, a bargain must be good for one of the parties, and bad for the other. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I hold very strongly to the view that there are three kinds of bargains. One in which both parties to the bargain. benefit, another where one of the parties benefits, and the other loses, and a third, where both parties are at a disadvantage as a result of the arrangement. It is my judgment that the arrangement embodied in this Bill, as between the province of Manitoba and the Dominion at large, is one of the latter class; it is not fair to Manitoba and it is not fair to the rest of the Dominion. Take for instance, and only as an illustration, the very simple provision in regard to the access of the province of Ontario to a nort cn Hudson bay. The provision is in the first place, very remarkable.	It is not
unreasonable on the face that the province of Ontario should desire to have a port on Hudson bay. On the other hand it is not unreasonable that the province of Manitoba, whose trade must furnish the reason, and to all intents and purposes the only reason, for the existence of such a port, would desire to have provincial jurisdiction over that port. I do not intend to trouble the House with a discussion of the claims of Ontario, but as a western representative, looking at the matter from a western point of view, I am at a loss to know on what reasonable ground, except the desire for acquisition of territory, the province of Ontario has for the claim that it made. If it is asserted that the province of Ontario requires, or desires, a port on Hudson bay at the mouth of the Nelson river, as an outlet for the trade of the province, or as a tributary to that tradp. I can only say, that inasmuch as the railway connection of such a port with the present railway system of the eastern provinces, and of the province of Ontario at Cochrane, would involve the construction of a road some 800 miles in length through 137J
a territory which, at the present time, is not productive of traffic, the construction of such a road is an enterprise that it does not seem to me comes within the range of possibility so far as Ontario is concerned. It is not only that the road would be 800 miles in length, but even that is a matter for consideration even to the province of Ontario, but it is a fact that it would run in a direction to which the outbound traffic of the present productive portion of Ontario would never go; and in all human probability the traffic originated at that point which will find its ultimate market in the province of Ontario, would be so limited as would never warrant the construction of such a road. Notwithstanding this fact, under this very remarkable arrangement the province of Ontario is given proprietary rights in a strip of territory running through the proposed extension of the province of Manitoba and abutting on the proposed port of Nelson. If there is any value in that country at all, it is in whatever locality is fixed upon as the ultimate port is reached by the Hudson Bay railway to be constructed from the Saskatchewan river. If there is any value in that territory it is in the ownership of the town site at that port, which the government proposes under this Bill to hand over to the province of Ontario for the benefit and profit of that province without requiring any consideration from it for the proprietary rights given. It is true there is some mention of the possibility of the construction of a railroad, tout I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, how absurd such a possibility is, and there is nothing in the Bill, and there is nothing in the explanations that have been made, that indicate in the most remote degree the intention of the province )f Ontario to build a railway to that point. Why is this grant made? Is it done for the purpose of satisfying public opinion in the province of Ontario? No, it is to be for the purpose of strengthening the partisan position of the government of Ontario. This government sees fit to hand over to the government of Ontario the only piece of property of serious value in the proposed to be added territory, hand that piece of valuable property over to Ontario without rhyme or reason, without consideration of any kind whatever, simply as a partisan measure for the purpose of strengthening the partisan government in that province. In regard to the position of Manitoba, if that province is entitled to the jurisdiction over that territory and has to assume the responsibility and cost of administration within that territory, surely ithe province of Ontario has no claim, right, title or interest in the proprietorship of the only particularly valuable piece

of land, so far as we can see at -present in that whole area.
It is true that it would either be the property of the Dominion or of the province of Ontario, it would not be the property of the province of Manitoba under the arrangement made in the Bill. But I submit that if this piece of valuable property is to be taken from the Dominion and' handed over to one of the provinces, surely in common justice it should be handed over to the province within whose provincial jurisdiction it is situated, and the province whose trade is the one thing that will give it value. If the province of Ontario is to receive the benefit financially of the ocean port created by the trade of the province of Manitoba, _ while that port is within the jurisdiction of the province of Manitoba, it seems to me to be an arrangement that can neither be satisfactory to Ontario nor to Manitoba nor to the Dominion. If it. is right that the province of Ontario should have a port on Hudson Bay, then it was right that the boundaries should be so adjusted that the province of Ontario should exercise jurisdiction over the port that it was entitled to. It should exercise provincial jurisdiction over that port. It was an easy matter to arrange the boundaries so as to meet that condition. If the easterly boundary of the province of Manitoba had been extended eastward, north of the English river where it does not interfere with the present province of Ontario, if it had been extended easterly to longitude 53J west, there would have been a straight easterly boundary between Ontario and Manitoba north of the English river that would have given to Ontario the south side of the Nelson river at the proposed port of Nelson, it would have given that province the jurisdiction over the port that presumably it is entitled to have. I say that when the -province of Ontario does not get jurisdiction over the port that this Bill says it is entitled to, and the province of Manitoba does not get the port over which this Bill gives it jurisdiction, it seems to me to be an absolutely fixed conclusion that the arrangement is neither fair to Manitoba, nor to Ontario, nor yet to the Dominion.
In regard to the subsidy again, I say that it is not only possible, but it is a fact that the subsidy arrangement can at the same time be unfair to Manitoba and unfair to the sister provinces. On what grounds is it claimed that the debt account of Manitoba should be increased by reason of the increase of population?	What is the
population of Manitoba?	455,614.	The
province of British Columbia has a population of 392,480, and it gets an allowance on debt account, so I am informed, on a population of 60,000. That is to say, the Mr. OLIVER.
province of British Columbia with a much larger area than the enlarged- province of Manitoba, with a population nearly as large, will receive a subsidy on debt account on one fourth as many people as the province of Manitoba will under this arrangement, while she has a population very nearly equal to that of Manitoba. Is that fair to the province of British Columbia? If justice is to be done, this Bill should have contained provisions for an increase of subsidy on debt account to the province of British Columbia as well as to the province of Manitoba. I followed what my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) said about the right and propriety of increasing the allowance on debt account to the various provinces proportioned to the increase of population. In taking that position he was following the position that I myself took in the debate on the presentation of the resolution. I quite agree, as a representative of the western country, where the population has increased rapidly, and in the nature of things must increase very largely over the present population-it is elimentary that an arrangement whereby the subsidy on debt account is fixed on a certain low basis of population, is not fair to those provinces as they increase largely in population. Even at the present time, take the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba with the proposed increases; they are getting an allowance on debt account for 250,000 when the population ranges from 375,000, in the case of Alberta, 392,000 in the case of British Columbia, 455,000 in the case of Manitoba, and 492,000 in the case of Saskatchewan. Now, if there is to be a readjustment of the debt account of the province of Manitoba because of increase of population-I do not for an instant say there should not be such a readjustment,-I say there is absolutely the same ground, and a very much stronger ground, for readjustment in the case of British Columbia, an absolutely stronger ground even to-day; there are stronger grounds to-day for an adjustment of the allowance on debt account in respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan. What we contend is that when the government undertakes to deal with this question of debt account they should1 deal with it having due regard to the rights of all the provinces, and not, as my hon. friend from St. John has said, pick out one province to be dealt with as a matter of special favour and special right, and ignore the conditions and the position of the other provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
Did the hon. gentleman think that way when he was arranging with Alberta and Saskatchewan? Why

did he not give a consideration then for the debt account to the other provinces?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: The debt accounts of Alberta and Saskatchewan were fixed at the time those provinces entered confederation on the basis of the then estimated population, just as the present debt allowance to the province of Manitoba was fixed under the then estimated population.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: What about British Columbia?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: It was fixed exactly the same way, on the then estimated population. It was perfectly right according to the conditions as they then existed.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: My hon. friend's point is that there was an unfairness toward British Columbia, which was altogether wrong, existing in 1905, when the arrangement was made with Alberta and Saskatchewan. Why -was it not corrected?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
I was not dealing with British Columbia as connected with Alberta and Saskatchewan. The late government dealt with Alberta and Saskatchewan as new provinces coming into the confederation, and they gave those provinces an allowance on debt account which was 'based on the then estimated actual population of these provinces, which is exactly what was done with British Columbia and what was done in the beginning with Manitoba. But, from time to time, as my hon. friend has stated, the debt account of Manitoba was increased with the increase of population until the readjustment of 1885, when an estimated population of 125,000 was taken. But, a very large increase in population has taken place since that time, an increase that was not expected, that was not looked for, that was not hoped for, and that never would have occurred if my hon. friends had not given place in 1896 to a more capable administration; and had it not been for that increase in population this allowance of debt account would not have been so far behind the requirements as it is now. But, we are facing in this matter, a new condition, a condition which has arisen since 1905, a condition that requires to be dealt with, that this government is dealing with in one way, but that we say should not be dealt with in that way, but should be dealt with in a more comprehensive way, in a way that would do justice not only to Manitoba hut also to Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, to say nothing about the eastern provinces. For the purpose of argument I am leaving the case of the eastern provinces to be dealt with by other members. It is not only the fact that Saskatchewan to-day, according to the last census, has1 a population twice as great ias (the population on which it is receiving allowance on debt account,
but that population, and the population cr\ Al'berta, are increasing, as the census returns show, more rapidly than the population of any other province in the Dominion. Therefore, if their allowance on debt account to-day is below what it ought to be, if their debt account is to remain at the present figure, it is going to be still further -and further below every succeeding year. When the government undertakes to deal with this question of debt account in regard to Manitoba on the plea that it wants to do justice, we ask that it shall fio justice by other provinces as well as Manitoba.
Agakij let me repeat what I said on a former occasion, that the simple statement of area, of population and of subsidy figures, does not establish an equality of treatment. To-day the part of Manitoba that is effectively occupied, on which the provincial government is required to expend money in .enforcing its jurisdiction, is less than half the present area of the province. The present area of the province is some 73,000 square miles. Everybody knows that the population of the province occupies less than the south-west half of the total area. There is a part of the present province of Manitoba-I speak of the north-eastern portion-which is as little known to the government of Manitoba as the Congo is in the interior of Africa.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: What portion of the northeastern part of Manitoba ?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: My hon. friend is more familiar with the geography of that country than I am.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I think I am.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: I say that over the greater portion of that area northeast of Lake Winnipeg the provincial government exercises no more jurisdiction than it does over the Congo Free State.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext: It is a very small area.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
It is not a small area. My hon. friend can see on the map that this is not a small area. This is a statement of fact, and I want to compare that condition with that of Saskatchewan which is effectively occupied by population requiring the administration of the provincial government from the boundary line to a point north of Prince Albert, a distance of not less than 300 miles. There is more territory at present effectively occupied in the province of Saskatchewan than the total present area of Manitoba. Everybody knows that. What is true of Saskatchewan is true in a still greater degrge of Alberta. There is a much greater area in Alberta effectively occupied and requiring provincial expenditure and administration than there is in the whole province of Manitoba. Yet, from the Dominion treasury the prov-

inces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are to get only as much as the province of Manitoba is to get under this arrangement. We do not complain of that if it is the arrangement that exists because of having been entered into years ago, and it is considered not desirable to disturb it, but when this government undertakes to disturb tint arrangement and disturb it in the name of justice and fair play we ask for justice and fair-play all round. Let it be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Manitoba between one-fourth and one-third of the population is in the city of Winnipeg. The cost of provincial administration in the city of Winnipeg is trifling compared with the cost of administration in connection with a like population in the agricultural portions of the country. It is a fact that outside the city of Winnipeg the province of Manitoba has not increased seriously in population in the past few years, or at any rate, has not increased in comparison with Saskatchewan and Alberta. Its increase is in the city of Winnipeg. Does this government tell us that, because of an increase in population in the city of Winnipeg, where there is no practical increase in cost to the provincial government in the matter of administration, the province of Manitoba should have an increased allowance on debt account when the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, whose cost of administration is increased stupendously by a similar increase of population, should have no consideration on debt account? If there ie to be justice and fair-play in this matter we ask for justice and fair-play. We are prepared to accede to an arrangement for ian increased debt allowance to the other western provinces including British Columbia, having regard to the physical conditions which lay immeasurably heavier burdens upon the administration in those provinces than are laid upon Manitoba, or will be laid upon that province by this addition of territory.
In regard to the increased subsidy on land account, there are matters that have to be considered in that connection that are aside from and, in my judgment, far above in importance the mere matter of the amount of money that is to be paid.
First of all, let us clear away some little misapprehension which I think exists as to the amount of increase of subsidy on land account that the province of Manitoba is to receive. At present the subsidy of the province, (as shown in the estimates this year) is $833,838, but there must be added to that the amount that is derived by the province from the sale of swamp an'd university lands, which, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, is $149,230, and this brings the total amount that the province of Manitoba is to-day realizing from subsid-Mr. OLIVER.
ies received from this Dominion to $983,068. Under the arrangement proposed by the Bill the province will have $190,000 for civil government, $364,491 per capita, $562,500 on land account, and $381,584 on debt account, a total of $1,498,575, against $983,068 that it is now receiving, or a difference of $515,507. But let me remind the House that under the arrangement that was offered to Manitoba by the Liberal government, there was to be an annual payment of $200,000, so that if that is deducted, the advantage of cash that comes to the province of Manitoba on land account over and above what would have come to the province under the offer made by the Liberal government is, $315,507. That is, the province is better off in cash by reason of this arrangement over and above what it would have received, had the offer of the late Liberal government been accepted, by $315,507, but it is worse off by eight million acres of swamp land, according to the estimate given by the Minister of Finance.

speechtext: My hon. friend is behind the lighthouse altogether. The condition now is: that this offer by the present government is $315,000 better in cash and eight million acres worse in swamp lands than the offer of the Liberai government. I think it will take all the gymnastic ability-I mean gymnastic ability in figures-of the Minister of Finance to explain how $315,000 in cash each year is better for the province than an asset of eight million acres of land, some 880,000 acres of which have been sold at a net profit to the province as we are informed, of $2,684,601.

That is how this bargain figures out now as compared with the offer made by 'the Liberal government less than a year ago.

The total acreage sold is stated to have been 838,484-16 acres; tihe amount received for them is $3,137,399.30.
