so oq. At the time of confederation there were four classes of subsidies recognized and only four, and there has been one added since. There was, in the first class, a sum allotted to each province for government and legislation, secondly, there was provision for allowing 80 cents per head of the population, thirdly, there was provision ior paying the several provinces certain *sums growing out of the allowance for debt, and in the fourth class, there were special grants. Now I have been unable from the statutes, to ascertain any very definite principle upon which any of these allowances were made. If you look at the Act *of 1867, you will find in the first place, that ihe debt allowed the old province of Canada, which was composed of Ontario and QueDec, was $62,500,000, to the province of Nova Scotia, $8,000,000 and to the province [DOT]of New Brunswick $7,000,000. There is a special grant allowed in the British North America Act for New Brunswick. That Act provides that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec should be allowed 80 cents per head of their population, based upon the population of 1861. Now that was not made applicable under the British North America Act to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, for you will find in section 118 of the British North America Act. these words:
The following sums shall be paid yearly by Canada to the several provinces for the support of their governments and legislatures

The amounts are guaranteed and the section continues:
-and an annual grant in aid of each province shall be made equal to eighty cents per head of the population as ascertained by the census of one thousand eight hundred and sixty-one, and in the case of Nova Scotia and Xmv Brunswick the 80 cents per head was to be based on the decennial census.
They had not adhered to the same principle which was applied to Ontario and Quebec.
-by each subsequent decennial census until the population of each of those two provinces amounts to four hundred thousand souls, at which rate such grant shall thereafter remain.
Now there is a special provision in the Act of 1867 which is applicable to Nova ocotia and New Brunswick and not made applicable to Quebec'and Ontario. Then you have a special grant made to New Brunswick by this very Act in the very next section:
New Brunswick shall receive by half-yearly payments in advance from Canada for a period of ten years from the Union an additional allowance of sixty-three thousand dollars per annum

On what principle? There is nothing in the Act to indicate.	*

maintopic: SUPPLY OF CEMENT TO DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
speechtext:
-but as long as the public debt of that province remains under seven million dollars, a deduction equal to the interest at five per centum per annum on .such deficiency shall be made from that allowance of sixty-three thousand dollars.
Then I find after the union there were some special grants, and I may say that each one of these four classes has been modified from time to time. The sum allowed for government and legislation has been changed many times by statute. The sum allowed per head has been changed at .east once, even as to Ontario and Quebec. At the conference in 1906-it was agreed that the annua! sum for government and legislation should be $240,000 instead of $80,000, as it had been up to that time in the two provinces, and it was agreed also that their per capita allowance should, instead of being based on the population of 1861, be based upon the decennial census. The special grants have been changed. The debt allowance has been changed time and time again by special legislation.
The first special grant after confederation I find recorded was made to Nova Scotia in 1869, by chap. 2, 32-33 Vic. It was a grant of $82,695 a year. New Brunswick got the amount I mentioned a moment ago, $63,000 for ten years. In the case of Manitoba several changes have been made. Changes were made in 1873, 1874, 1884, and 1907. All these classes of subsidies have been varied from time to time by statute on special grounds. I cannot find any principle upon which they have gone. Now, we come to the present Bill. These three prairie provinces occupy a different position in confederation from that of the other provinces. The British North America Act, section 109, provides:
All lands, mines, minerals and royalties, belonging to the several provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at the union, and all sums then due or payable for suoh lands, mines, minerals or royalties, shall belong to the several provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in which the same are situate or arise subject to any trusts existing in respect thereof, and to any interest other than that of the province in the same.
But these three western provinces, out of the nine provinces of the Dominion, have been deprived of the public 'lands within their borders. Hence they are to be dealt with on a different basis altogether. Saskatchewan and Alberta, in 1905, were very generously dealt with. Manitoba now is asking, as being in the same class as the other two, to be dealt with on the same basis, and it is proposed by this Bill to do it. Now, 1 only repeat what I started with, that the hon. gentleman who began this criticism against this Bill has been completely and fully answered by hon. gentlemen who followed him on the other side,

and by the right honourable the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). In tlie first place, the plea that the other provinces are unfairly dealt with by giving this territory to Manitoba was completely answered by the speech of the present leader of the opposition on the 13th of July, 1908. The statement that too 'much money is being paid to Manitoba is answered by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who showed that the government of which he was a member, had offered Manitoba $885,000 more than is provided under this Bill.

speechtext:
If I were allowed to speak on another occasion my audience would bb fresher than at the present time. But if it is the desire of the leader of the House that 1 should speak on this occasion, I will do so.
It might have been thought that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meig-hen) having been put up to reply to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), he would be able to dispose of the argument of the hon. member for St. John in a way satisfactory to the government. But it is evident that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) regards the hon. member from St. John as not having been answered. He found the arguments of that hon. gentleman were too keen and cogent, too much to the point, and also that they were not answered by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, and he undertook to answer them himself. I must say, that if I am capable of following the line of argument presented by the Minister of Labour, it will be necessary to put up somebody else on that other side. If the hon. member for St. John was not answered by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie I can assure you if I am a judge at all, he stands still unanswered, and it is just as necessary now, as it was before to make a proper, a substantial and conclusive reply, if such a thing be possible, to the argument put forward by the hon. member for St. John. The point made by the hon. member for St. John was that somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3,000,000 was being paid to the province of Manitoba without the slightest justification either under the constitution or any form of law that we know of in this Dominion. And that point is still unanswered. As I have suggested, it will be necessary for the Minister of Finance himself, who is answerable to the people of this country for what shall become of the public revenue, to either give a satisfactory answer to the hon. gentleman
from St. John or strike this provision out of the Bill. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) said that some hon. members on this side were finding fault with the terms because they were too good and some because they were too bad. I submit that it does not make any difference whether the terms are good or bad when we are dealing with the provisions of the statutes under which we live.. If we make a bargain which must be governed by the constitution and have no right to break away from it and to make bargains and agreements that have no foundation in the conditions and terms of that constitution, I submit that a bargain in reference to the responsibilities of the citizens of this Dominion must not be governed by the generosity or wishes of any government which for the time being happens to be in power.
I submit that the rights of our provinces and of each citizen must be founded upon a better and more stable basis than that. We came into the family of confederation upon a well-defined basis and subject to conditions which were regarded as fair to all, and we have the right to suppose that whether we are in the maritime provinces or in British Columbia, whether the province to which we belong is washed by the surges of the Atlantic, or by the waves of the Pacific, the same laws must apply, and that the conditions under which we entered confederation shall be regarded and respected by the government.
I submit that the moment we depart from that principle, the moment we come, as the Minister of Finance said the other day, to be good-natured, the moment that it is a question of kindliness apart from the consideration of actual facts and conditions and the relations of the provinces to each other and to confederation, that moment we are treading on dangerous ground. The part of the British North America Act which deals with this particular point now under consideration is very simple and very easily understood. It is not necessary to go over the historical events to explain why we are dealing with Manitoba in this way. 1 was going to say that at the time of confederation it was discovered shortly afterwards that there were some grave doubts as to whether this parliament had the right to create provinces at all, or whether we had any right to make a constitutional compact with any territory, and create it into a province. It was found necessary to go back to the mother country for authority and get a new chapter to add to the British North America Act, and remove all question as to our right to create provinces. Under that Act we got the right to create provinces, to give them a constitution, and all the powers. I submit that we have no right to deal with

It does not make the slightest difference. But it was explained here that that was the mere correcting of a mistake in the arrangement ot the debt at the time. That was the reason why better terms were given to the province of Nova Scotia. But it is no answer to tell me that a certain thing was done if that thing was not constitutional. I suppose as we grow in population and strength, and as we become wiser in experience, we shall grow in knowledge of the constitution under which we live. I find in our constitution a provision which says that we can add to a province from time to time, and when we do add territory to a province we must make such financial arrangements as will compensate that province for the charges that have been brought about. But certainly we have no authority to go back to the foundation and disorganize that. That is the condition which I find here. I find that in the preamble of the Bill the idea I suggest has been to some extent followed, so far as the draftsman could, until he found it necessary to break away from it; that is, he was going to provide' for the necessities of the case where additional territory had been added to a province.
The preamble says:

Whereas, on the thirteenth day of July, one thousand nine hundred and eight, the House of Commons resolved that the limits of the province of Manitoba should be increased by the extension of the boundaries of the province northward to the sixtieth parallel of latitude and north-eastward to the shores of Hudson bay, as in the said resolution is more particularly set out, upon such terms and conditions as may he agreed to by the legislature, Manitoba and the parliament of Canada.
And whereas it is desirable that the financial terms

and accepted in that case or in this, then, of course, all that is necessary is that we pass an Act of this parliament that will override any of the terms of the constitution. Upon that basis and for these reasons I submit that we have no authority at all to change the terms of confederation or the terms upon which Manitoba entered confederation. Manitoba may have entered confederation on terms that were not satisfactory. Manitoba may have entered the confederation on terms that were not as good as they ought to be. Then, of course, there is a constitutional way of remedying the difficulty. That constitutional way, I presume, was followed, particularly in 1907, when at a conference of all the provinces of the Dominion a basis for the payment of subsidies to the provinces was agreed upon which was perfectly satisfactory to the present Premier of Manitoba and to the bon. gentleman who is now Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), and who was then an important member of the Manitoba government. They, at that time, agreed to the conditions that were accepted by this House and as to which an address was presented to His Majesty for legislation readjusting and reconstructing the terms of confederation. In 1907 the terms of confederation were constitutionally readjusted by an Act of the Imperial parliament which can be found in the Acts of 1908 of this parliament, and, that being the case, I think It is rather strange that now we are making another change, setting aside altogether everything that has been done from 1870 down to the present and taking a new standard for confederation. What is the standard that is taken now? The standard up to now was the proper adjustment of all our difficulties, financial and otherwise, under the terms of that Act.
If this Bill is founded on right and justice the inference from it is that we must start afresh and give new terms to ' every other province in the Dominion. I submit that there is no justification for acting in this way. I believe the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was perfectly within constitutional lines when he said that if we were to give better conditions to Manitoba it should only be done after the provinces had all sat down w'th the Dominion and heard the grievances of Manitoba, if grievances she had, and then make provision to remedy them. But, if each province of the Dominion can come to the government at Ottawa and get better conditions according to the pull it has with the government, and that seems to be the only rule now, where is it all going to end? We heard to-night that the fate of Manitoba could very well be left to the Premier of Manitoba, and acording to the Minister Mr. MoKENZIE.
of Labour, Mr. Rob'lin would see to it that his province received fair treatment at the hands of this government. We were also told that Sir James Whitney and the government of Ontario would see to it that Ontario was wrell treated, but that is not the spirit in which to deal with a great question of this kind, and that is not the way in which the people of this country would wish to have it dealt with. The people of Canada want to know whether or not we have a constitution in this country; they want to know whether there is going to be an equitable scale of division between the provinces, so that each province will be dealt with according to the understanding on which it entered confederation, and not because Mr. So-and-so and Mr. Some-body-else is more vigilant than another to look after its rights. I submit that there is no constitutional basis for this law and that it is simply a makeshift to get over a certain contingency in order to bolster up the Manitoba government and try and place the province in a better financial condition than it is in to-day. I wish that some one on the other side of the House, who knows something about the subject, would tell me where we find our authority for passing legislation such as this: where do we find a constitutional basis for reconstructing and making over again the financial terms we have accorded to the province of Manitoba? If it is true that we can do so with respect to Manitoba, what argument is there that we cannot do so in the case of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. If the Premier of New Brunswick, or of any other province, should come here to-morrow with a hard-up story stating that his province was not treated properly at confederation, that his debt allowance and his per capita allowance should be increased, in view of such legislation as this, how can we refuse his demand? I repeat that the reason I spoke on this question is to enter my protest against any manipulation of the standing of the different provinces in confederation without sufficient constitutional authority for it. I say the people of Canada will make a great mistake if they allow this tinkering with the right each province has under the British North America Act. I say that the people of Canada should demand that if changes are necessary with respect to the standing of any province in the confederation, these changes should be brought about in a constitutional wray and not in the extraordinary manner in which this Bill proposes.
